claims.text: The structural stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles during high-temperature catalytic operation is governed by enthalpic contributions from their constituent elements.
Systematically changing constituent-element ratios changes the enthalpic stability of the nanoparticles.
Changes in enthalpic stability cause variations in nanoparticle structural integrity at high temperature.
Elemental ratios can be optimized to provide greater structural stability than an equal-ratio baseline.
Nanoparticles with optimized elemental ratios will exhibit greater catalytic performance than nanoparticles with non-optimized ratios.
The relevant catalytic operating-temperature range is 773–1173 K.
The relevant thermoelectric-use temperature range is 473–1923 K.
Equal ratios of all constituent elements define the experimental baseline.
The proposed test varies elemental ratios while subjecting the resulting nanoparticles to high-temperature catalytic tests.
Structural integrity, catalytic activity, and thermal stability are the proposed measured responses.
The hypothesis is intended to apply only to multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
The exact relationship between elemental ratios and high-temperature structural stability is not fully understood.
